lines.text: Capstone time! You will use everything from Level 2 to design an AI helper for a real problem at your school.
Start with a real problem you have seen, like lost water bottles, confusing recycling bins or last-minute revision panic.
Name the user, like Grade 6 students or the school librarian.
Ask two or three people if the problem is real for them.
Write a spec: what goes in, what comes out, and the rules.
Decide what the AI does and what a human must still do.
Some parts are better without AI, and that is a smart choice too.
Build a small working version: app instructions, a short Python or Scratch program, a survey chart or a video.
Test it with normal, tricky and attack cases.
Fix what fails and record it.
Ask who could be harmed or left out, and what data you collect.
Check that it is honest, private and fair.
Write what the AI cannot do, so users do not over-trust it.
Tell the story in three minutes: the problem, the user, your solution, a live demo, what you tested and your ethics check.
End with what you would build next, and practise it with a timer.
Here are four capstone ideas, but the best one is a problem you have seen yourself.
Pick a problem that is real, small enough to prototype, and helps someone at school.
Riya tests her recycling guide with a tricky item: a used chips packet.
It confidently says the paper bin, but these packets are usually plastic and foil.
She adds the school’s real bin list to the instructions, and a rule to say ask a teacher when unsure.
Kabir asks the AI to act as a critical friend and find risks in his idea.
He checks each risk himself, keeps the useful ones, and adds them to his rules.
A strong pitch follows this route, from the problem to the next step, in three minutes.
The live demo is the star, so practise it, and have a screenshot ready in case the internet fails.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now plan it, build it, test it, and share it!
